extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, philosophers of science, and researchers learning inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting and evaluating inductive investigations (Methods of Agreement, Difference, Joint Method), handling plurality and intermixture of causes, and choosing deductive vs. experimental approaches. Focused on how to infer causes from observed instances and on pitfalls in experimental/observational design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement's characteristic imperfection
rubrics_metrics.description: If two instances agree only in antecedent A, it might be concluded that A is an invariable antecedent of a; but this conclusion tacitly assumes the same cause produced a in both instances, which fails if there can be a plurality of causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When only a few instances are compared, conclusions from the Method of Agreement have little real value except as suggestions. They should lead to experiments applying the Method of Difference or to deductive reasoning connecting the result with established laws. If plurality of causes is possible, agreement across few cases may be mere coincidence; multiply and vary instances to strengthen the presumption in favour of A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference sufficiency and robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: If one instance (BC) yields b c and adding A (ABC) yields a b c, then in that instance A was either the cause of a or an indispensable portion of its cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Method of Difference is not diminished by plurality of causes: two instances (one positive and one negative) are sufficient for a complete and rigorous induction in that case. Use positive and negative instances to establish causal role of a circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference (Indirect Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: When instances in which a is present agree only in containing A, and instances in which a is absent agree only in not containing A, A must be not only the cause but the only possible cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This joint method has an immense advantage over simple Agreement because the negative premiss ensures exclusivity of cause. In observational sciences with limited experimental control, this method is a primary resource. Negative instances are especially valuable though often harder to obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of variation over mere number of instances
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency of unscientific inquirers is to rely too much upon number: most people hold conclusions with assurance proportioned to mass of experience rather than analysis of instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding instances of the same kind (differing only in recognized immaterial points) adds nothing to evidence. A single instance that eliminates some antecedent common to others is more valuable than many similar instances. First assure no error in individual facts by repetition without variation; once assured, vary circumstances to exclude alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative instances are difficult but necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the Method of Agreement to negative instances (those in which a phenomenon does not take place) is in principle free from the characteristic imperfection affecting affirmative Agreement, but generally impossible without positive instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is often more feasible to seek resemblance among the comparatively few definite positive instances and then examine whether the absence of that circumstance corresponds to negative instances. Exhausting the field of negation is usually impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting plurality of causes (actual plurality)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an effect is really producible by two or more causes, these may be discovered either as separate sequences (different sets of instances showing different causes) or by failing to find any single antecedent common to all instances and instead finding that one or other of several antecedents is always present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a common element can be detected among the alternatives, we may ascend to a single operative cause; otherwise list the different antecedents as distinct causes, each sufficient by itself to produce the effect. Look for separate lines of observation/experimentation for each suspected cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermixture of effects — transformation vs composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrence of causes that interferes may take two forms: (a) transformation — separate effects cease and a qualitatively new phenomenon appears (chemical example); (b) composition — separate effects continue and are compounded (mechanical forces), producing a sum that may disguise individual contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation cases are generally amenable to experiment and analysis (e.g., water ↔ hydrogen + oxygen). Composition cases are much harder for direct induction because separate effects may cancel or merge; deduction is often required to unravel them, with experiments supplying premisses rather than full solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical analysis as detection of causes among effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Some compounds reproduce their component agents under certain conditions, so the causes of a phenomenon may be found among its effects (e.g., decomposition of water yields hydrogen and oxygen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experiments that reverse or decompose the phenomenon (Lavoisier example) to reveal component causes. Where reappearance of agents occurs, analysis by experiment can discover the causes as effects of the compound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heteropathic mental effects require synthetic study of constituents
rubrics_metrics.description: For heteropathic laws of mind (complex passions or emotions formed by coalition of simpler impulses), the factors cannot generally be re-produced from the product and so cannot be discovered by decomposing the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discover these laws by studying the simple feelings themselves and ascertaining synthetically, through experimenting on various combinations, what complex states they can generate. Direct decomposition is not available here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of causes frequently eludes experimental detection
rubrics_metrics.description: When causes compound their effects (composition), the separate effects are intermingled and often disguised, so observation may fail to trace any fixed relation between causes and the resulting phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the whole assemblage of concurrent causes as a single cause if attempting experimental ascertainment, but recognize the limitations. For many such cases deduction (a priori reasoning from the laws of separate causes) is the natural method; experiments can try combinations but may not isolate constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express causal laws as tendencies, not absolute results
rubrics_metrics.description: Because causes are liable to be counteracted, laws of causation should be stated affirmatively of tendencies only, not of actual results (e.g., say an object 'tends to move' rather than 'moves').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer terminology that captures tendency (pressure in mechanics) rather than asserting actual motion; this avoids apparent exceptions and better matches how laws operate when counteracting causes are present. Guard formulations to accommodate counteraction (e.g., 'tends to' or 'unless prevented').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid calling concurrent principles 'exceptions'
rubrics_metrics.description: What is thought to be an exception to a principle is usually some other distinct principle or force acting concurrently; there is not a law and an exception, but multiple laws acting together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not divide cases between a rule and its 'exception'; recognize concurrent principles each extending to all cases. Re-framing purported exceptions as concurrent causes avoids superficial categorization and clarifies causal analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three general methods for studying complex effects: a priori, observation, experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of an effect produced by composition of causes may be discovered: (1) deductively (a priori) from the laws of the separate causes; (2) by pure observation collating instances of the effect; (3) experimentally by operating on the causes and trying combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduction is naturally suited when the laws of constituents are known; pure observation suits when collating instances is feasible; experiment attempts combinations of causes to hit the producing assemblage. Select the method according to the case's amenability (illustrated by the planned example of medicine/health).
